newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin says euro conditions not against Maastricht.
newsitem.headline: Jospin says euro conditions not against Maastricht.

text.p: French Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin said on Tuesday that his party's conditions for France's entry into the European Monetary Union did not conflict with the terms of the Maastricht Treaty.
But he declined to say whether or not a Socialist government would enter the EMU on schedule on January 1, 1999, or if it would respect all the criteria.

"In Germany, there are authorative institutes which doubt that Germany can meet the three percent budget deficit target, or even the 60 percent debt target as result of the costs of the reunification. Everywhere the debate is open," Jospin told France 2 television in an interview.
The Maastricht Treaty made allowances for seeing the convergence criteria would be used as a "trend" instead of absolute figures, he said.
"The criteria are not in doubt. It's the application of the criteria. The Maastry Treaty envisages the application in trends. It's a matter of convergence," he said.
His party's call for an economic government as a counterweight to the European central bank was also possible within the pact.
"Maastricht does not say that you cannot have an economic government against the central bank. There is the possibility (in the treaty) if the governments want it," he said.
The stability pact agreed during the Dublin summit late last year, was not in line with the Maastricht Treaty.
"The Maastricht Treaty does not say that there has to be a stability pact. The one accepted by the Dublin summit is contrary to the Maastricht Treaty. We need a growth pact," Jospin said.

Jospin's remarks seemed to be aimed at countering suggestion that a Socialist government would try to renegotiate the Maastricht Treaty by saying his government would instead negotiate the application of the Treaty.

Earlier on Tuesday, at the presentation of a joint electoral declaration with the Communist Party for the parliamentary election of May 25 and June 1, Jospin said: "We are in favour of monetary union, but we don't want a dogmatic reading of the Maastricht Treaty."
